count/bytes: Computers store text as bytes, and a byte has only two hundred fifty-six possible values. So a vocabulary can start with two hundred fifty-six tokens, ids zero to two hundred fifty-five, and spell any text at all.
count/long: Here is a short text: hug, hugs, pug, run together. Ten bytes, so ten tokens. It works, but it is long.
count/pairs: Byte-pair encoding shortens it. Count every pair of neighboring tokens, left to right.
count/top: u followed by g comes up three times: more than any other pair.
count/merge: So merge it. u g becomes one new token, with the next free id, two hundred fifty-six, and every u g in the text is replaced.
count/shorter: Each replacement turns two tokens into one. Three replacements save three tokens: ten become seven.
repeat/again: Then do it again, on the new text. Now h followed by u g is the top pair, twice.
repeat/hug: It becomes token two hundred fifty-seven, the whole word hug, and seven tokens become five.
repeat/grow: Every merge adds exactly one token to the vocabulary. Merge zero made two hundred fifty-six and merge one made two hundred fifty-seven, so after k merges there are two hundred fifty-six plus k.
repeat/real: Real tokenizers run tens of thousands of merges. Fifty thousand of them make a vocabulary of fifty thousand two hundred fifty-six, where common words are single tokens.
repeat/rows: And every new token gets an id of its own, so a row of its own in the embedding table.
